Cryptococcosis Cryptococcosis is an infection caused by inhalation of the fungus Cryptococcus neoformans. It is rare in immuno- competent individuals, but is an important life-threatening disease in immunocompromised patients, especially those with AIDS, in whom it occurs principally as cryptococcal meningitis. Mild infections in immunocompetent patients may resolve without treatment, but oral fluconazole is usually effective if treatment is necessary.1 Itraconazole is a suitable alterna- tive in patients unable to take fluconazole. In either case, treatment should continue for several months. For more severe disease, amphotericin B may be given alone, or, if there is CNS involvement, with flucytosine. Patients may be switched to oral fluconazole after 2 weeks of induction therapy with amphotericin B and flucytosine or may con- tinue on amphotericin B and flucytosine for 6 to 10 weeks.1 Cryptococcosis in immunocompromised patients other than those with HIV infection should be treated as for CNS infections in immunocompetent patients.1 HIV-infected patients who develop cryptococcosis always require treatment. Those with isolated pulmonary or uri- nary-tract disease may be treated with oral fluconazole or, if fluconazole is not an option, itraconazole.1 A further al- ternative is combined treatment with fluconazole and flu- cytosine for 10 weeks followed by maintenance with flu- conazole, although the toxicity of this regimen limits its usefulness. Those with more severe disease may be given intravenous amphotericin B until symptoms are controlled and then switched to oral fluconazole.1-3 Patients with HIV infection who develop cryptococcal meningitis should re- ceive induction therapy with intravenous amphotericin B and intravenous flucytosine.1-3 Amphotericin B may be given alone in patients unable to tolerate flucytosine. In re- fractory cases, amphotericin B may be given intrathecally or intraventricularly. Oral fluconazole and intravenous flu- cytosine is an alternative to the use of amphotericin B but carries a high risk of toxicity.
